opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's a reasonable thing to do, but I'd be careful about how much security you think it actually buys you.

There's a long history in security of people assuming that hiding something makes it safe, and it almost never works out the way they hope. Keeping the weights private does raise the bar. If I can't download the model, I can't run gradient-based attacks directly, I can't fine-tune away the safety training, and I can't poke at it a million times for free on my own hardware. Those are real benefits and I don't want to dismiss them.

But a lot of the attacks we care about don't actually need the weights. Adversarial examples transfer: you can build an attack on an open model you control, and a surprising fraction of the time it works on the closed one too. You can also attack through the API alone. Some of my own work showed that you can extract nontrivial information about a production model, like parts of its architecture or specific parameters, just by querying it cleverly. So "it's behind an API" doesn't mean "it's a black box you can learn nothing about."

The other issue is that secrecy is fragile. If your security argument rests on the weights never leaking, you've got one point of failure. Weights can be stolen, an insider can walk out with them, a partner can get breached. When that happens, every protection you were counting on vanishes at once. Compare that to a system that's robust even when the attacker knows everything about it, which is what we'd really want.

So my view is that proprietary deployment is a useful layer: it slows people down, lets you monitor usage, and lets you patch and rate limit. It's good defense in depth. What I worry about is people treating it as the thing that makes the model secure. The model itself is still vulnerable, and you're mostly just making the vulnerabilities somewhat more annoying to find. For the stakes we're heading toward, I'd want security that doesn't depend on the attacker being unable to see how the system works.

r001.rationale: The response calls proprietary deployment a useful layer but does not present it as the best achievable strategy if deep learning cannot be secured.

r002.rationale: It mentions attacks transferring from open models, but does not say public scrutiny of disclosed methods could improve robustness.

r003.rationale: It wants security that does not depend on attackers being unable to see the system; it does not express a desire for release decisions to stop depending on security concerns.

r004.rationale: It explicitly says the model itself remains vulnerable and that proprietary deployment mainly makes vulnerabilities harder to find.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of those questions where people conflate two things that are actually quite different. There's "is the model proprietary," meaning you can't download the weights, and there's "is the model secure," meaning can someone make it do things you don't want it to do. And the history of security pretty much everywhere else tells us those two things are much less correlated than you'd hope.

The analogy I keep coming back to is cryptography. In the nineteenth century, Kerckhoffs wrote down this principle that a system should be secure even if everything about it except the key is public knowledge. And the reason we believe that isn't because secrecy has zero value. It's that secrecy is fragile. It's the kind of thing that gets lost once, and then you have nothing. Whereas if your system is actually secure, it stays secure even after the details leak.

So when someone says, "we keep our model closed and that's part of our security story," my first reaction is, okay, what does closed actually buy you? And the honest answer is it buys you a little bit. If I have the weights, I can run gradient-based attacks directly. I can find adversarial examples, I can find jailbreak strings that are optimized against the exact model. If I only have an API, I have to do black-box attacks, which are more expensive and noisier. So there's a real cost increase for the attacker. I don't want to pretend there isn't.

But the cost increase is maybe a constant factor. It's not a categorical change. We've shown over and over that you can take attacks optimized on open models and they transfer to closed models surprisingly well. We've shown you can do query-based attacks that steal parts of a model through its API. The stuff you can do with just query access is really quite a lot. So if your security model is "nobody can attack us because they can't see inside," that model is already broken, you just haven't noticed yet.

And then there's the flip side, which I think people underweight. Keeping things closed also keeps out the people who would find your problems and tell you about them. A huge fraction of what we know about how these models fail came from academics poking at open models, because that's what they could get their hands on. If the only people who can study your model in depth are your own employees, you've shrunk the set of people looking for bugs by orders of magnitude, and you've mostly kept the honest ones out. The sophisticated adversary who really wants in is going to get in anyway, or just steal the weights outright.

So my overall assessment is something like: proprietary is a legitimate business decision, and it's a legitimate choice for other reasons, maybe you think the capabilities are dangerous and you don't want them freely available. Fine. But as a security mechanism it's mostly a speed bump. It should be the thing you layer on top of a system you already believe is robust, not the thing you're relying on. If you find yourself saying "it's okay that this defense is weak because nobody can see it," that's the sentence that should worry you.

r001.rationale: The response calls proprietary status a speed bump and a possible business choice, but does not present it as the best achievable strategy if deep learning cannot be secured.

r002.rationale: It says academic study of open models has revealed failures and that closed models keep many potential bug-finders out, identifying scrutiny as a way to uncover problems that can support robustness.

r003.rationale: The response says proprietary decisions may be made for other reasons, but does not express a desire for release decisions to stop depending on security concerns.

r004.rationale: It says secrecy does not prevent attacks, transferred attacks work against closed models, and sophisticated adversaries may still get the weights—conveying that vulnerabilities can remain intact.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to ask what threat you’re trying to defend against. Keeping a model proprietary can make some attacks harder because an attacker doesn’t have the weights and can’t run unlimited experiments locally. That’s a real advantage. But it’s very different from saying the model is secure.

If the vulnerability is that someone can send the model an input that makes it do something you didn’t intend, putting it behind an API doesn’t necessarily fix that. The attacker still has access to the interface where the vulnerability exists. You can monitor usage, impose rate limits, and update the system, which are useful defenses, but those are concrete mechanisms you should evaluate individually.

There’s also a tradeoff: keeping the model closed limits who can study it and find problems. So I wouldn’t say openness automatically makes a model secure either. I’d want evidence about particular attacks and particular defenses. Proprietary access can be one layer of protection; it shouldn’t be the foundation of your security argument.

r001.rationale: The response calls proprietary access one layer of protection and says it should not be the foundation; it does not present lockdown as the best achievable strategy if deep learning cannot be secured.

r002.rationale: It says keeping a model closed limits who can study it and find problems, but does not identify public scrutiny of disclosed methods as a route to improving robustness.

r003.rationale: The response does not express a desire for release decisions to stop depending on security concerns.

r004.rationale: It says an API does not necessarily fix a vulnerability in the model: an attacker can still use the interface where that vulnerability exists.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish between making a model harder to attack and making it secure. Keeping the weights private does take away some capabilities from an attacker. They can’t inspect the model directly, compute gradients, or run unlimited experiments locally. Those are real advantages for the defender.

But I would be very skeptical of treating that as the security guarantee. If your model is accessible through an API, people can still experiment with it, discover failures, and share attacks. The fact that they don’t have the weights doesn’t mean they can’t find inputs that cause behavior you didn’t intend.

There’s also a tradeoff: keeping everything private makes it harder for independent researchers to understand the failures and help fix them. So I wouldn’t say that releasing weights has no security implications. It clearly does. But “we kept the model secret” is a much weaker claim than “we built a system that remains secure when someone deliberately tries to break it.”

r001.rationale: The response says private weights can limit attackers, but does not present proprietary lockdown as the best achievable strategy if deep learning cannot be made secure.

r002.rationale: It says independent researchers could understand failures and help fix them, but does not identify public scrutiny of disclosed model methods as a route to improving robustness.

r003.rationale: The response does not express a desire for security concerns to stop influencing model release decisions.

r004.rationale: It explains that keeping weights private does not prevent people from finding inputs that trigger unintended behavior, indicating the underlying vulnerabilities can remain.
